sections.content_markdown: In the $\text{NaH}$ molecule, $\text{Na}$ atom donates an electron to get the electronic configuration of inert gas and becomes $\text{Na}^{+}$ with $8$ electrons.

The $\text{H}$ atom accepts that electron to get the electronic configuration of an inert gas and become $\text{H}^{-}$ with $2$ electrons.

$$\text{Na} \longrightarrow \text{Na}^{+} + \text{e}^{-}$$
$$\text{H} + \text{e}^{-} \longrightarrow \text{H}^{-}$$
Now, $\text{Na}^{+}$ and $\text{H}^{-}$ come closer to form an ionic bond.

In the $\text{CaO}$ molecule, $\text{Ca}$ atom donates two electrons to get the electronic configuration of inert gas and becomes $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ with $8$ electrons.

$$\text{Ca} \longrightarrow \text{Ca}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^{-}$$

The $\text{O}$ atom accepts those electrons to get the electronic configuration of inert gas and become $\text{O}^{2-}$ with $8$ electrons.

$$\text{O} + 2\text{e}^{-} \longrightarrow \text{O}^{2-}$$
Now, $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{O}^{2-}$ come closer to form an ionic bond.

Notably, the metals belonging to Group 1 and 2 and the non-metals of Group 16 and 17 of the periodic table usually commit themselves to ionic bonding. Each rule has some exceptions. Here in this case, $\text{Al}$ of Group-13 commits itself to ionic bonding. Other elements do not show this tendency to donate or accept electrons as they have too many electrons at their outermost energy level. As ionic bonding takes place through electrostatic force, it is very strong.
